how-to-build-a-plumbing-flat-rate-price-.text:
Plumber Flat-Rate Price Calculator · guide

How to build a plumbing flat-rate price book: true hourly cost, parts markup and margin

Short answer: work out what one billable hour truly costs you, multiply by the hours the job takes including the drive, divide by one minus the margin you want, add the parts at a tiered markup and round up. The calculator does it for your own numbers and builds a whole price book you can export as CSV.

Everything below is arithmetic on invented numbers. Not business, tax, legal or licensing advice. Costs, prices and rules belong to your shop and your area. No warranty.

Step 1: your true cost per billable hour

Take a plumber paid $35 an hour with 25 percent burden (payroll tax, workers' comp, benefits): $43.75 an hour loaded. Over 2,080 paid hours that is $91,000.00 a year, but only 1,300 hours a year are sold, so each billable hour carries $70.00 of wages. Add $15,000 of truck, $6,000 of insurance, $3,500 of tools and $14,500 of phone, software, licence, office and marketing: $39,000 a year, or $30.00 per billable hour. The true cost is $100.00 an hour.

The billable-hours figure does most of the damage. Count every paid hour as billable and the cost looks like $62.50 an hour; at 1,000 billable hours it is $130.00.

Step 2: count the drive and the supplier run

A job with 2 hours on site, 0.75 hours of travel and a parts run is 2.75 hours of your day. At $100.00 that is $275.00 of time cost. A flat rate has to carry the travel; there is no line to add it on afterwards.

Step 3: margin on time, markup on parts

At a 30 percent margin the time charge is $275.00 / 0.70 = $392.86. Parts cost $120.00 and are marked up on tiers like tax brackets: 100 percent on the first $25, 60 percent from $25 to $100, 40 percent from $100 to $500 and 25 percent above that. That is $25.00 + $45.00 + $8.00 = $78.00 of markup, so the parts charge is $198.00.

Step 4: round up and check

$392.86 + $198.00 = $590.86, rounded up to the next $5 is $595.00. Your cost is $395.00, so the job leaves $200.00, a margin of 33.6%, and an effective $172.73 an hour after parts.

  • The minimum callout is the travel plus your shortest visit, 1.25 hours, with no parts: $180.00.
  • The flat price stops covering your cost at 4.75 hours. At 4.125 hours (50 percent over) it leaves $62.50; at 5.5 hours (double) it loses $75.00.

A big job: the water heater swap

3.5 hours on site, 1 hour of travel and $900.00 of parts. The time cost is $450.00 and the time charge $642.86. The parts markup is $25.00 + $45.00 + $160.00 + $100.00 = $330.00, so parts are charged at $1,230.00 and the job prices at $1,875.00. Cost is $1,350.00, the profit is $525.00 and the margin is 28.0% because the rounding and the lower tier on the big part both pull it away from the 30 percent aimed at time; the effective rate is $216.67 an hour after parts.

How to measure your own numbers

  • Add up a year of truck payments, fuel, repairs, insurance, tools, licence, phone, software and marketing from your statements.
  • Count billable hours from invoices, not from the calendar: divide hours you invoiced by weeks worked.
  • Time ten real jobs door to door, including the supplier run, before you set a book time for them.
  • Check your local licensing, permit and written-estimate rules before you publish a price book.

Common questions

How do I build a plumbing flat-rate price book?

List your common jobs, give each an honest on-site time, travel time and parts cost, then price every one the same way: true cost per billable hour times hours, divided by one minus your margin, plus parts at a tiered markup, rounded up. On the default numbers a 2.75-hour job with $120.00 of parts prices at $595.00.

Why must overhead be spread over billable hours and not paid hours?

Because only billable hours earn money. On the defaults $70.00 of wages and burden and $30.00 of truck, insurance, tools and overhead make a true cost of $100.00 per billable hour. Assume every one of the 2,080 paid hours is billable and the same job prices at $445.00; at 1,000 billable hours it needs $710.00.

How should I mark up plumbing parts?

Many shops use a sliding scale so small parts carry a high percentage and big parts a low one. On the default tiers $120.00 of parts earns $78.00 of markup, an effective 65.0%, and $900.00 of parts earns $330.00, an effective 36.7%.

Is this advice?

No. It is arithmetic on invented numbers; check every figure against your own records. Not business, tax, legal or licensing advice. No warranty.

Common questions

How do I work out a flat-rate price for a plumbing job?

Take your true cost per billable hour, multiply by the hours the job takes including travel, divide by one minus your target margin, then add the parts at cost plus a tiered markup and round up. On the default numbers a 2.75-hour job with $120.00 of parts at a true cost of $100.00 an hour prices at $595.00, which leaves $200.00 (33.6%). Enter your own figures; the defaults are invented.

What is my true cost per hour as a plumber?

Your loaded wage spread over the hours you can actually bill, plus truck, insurance, tools and overhead over the same hours. On the defaults that is $70.00 for wages and burden plus $30.00 of truck, insurance, tools and overhead, $100.00 for every billable hour, because only 1,300 of 2,080 paid hours are sold.

What should my minimum callout price be?

The travel time plus your shortest visit, at true cost and your margin, rounded up. On the defaults that is 1.25 hours and $180.00 before any parts.

Is a flat rate better than time and materials?

It depends on how reliably you estimate hours. On the defaults the flat price of $595.00 leaves $200.00 if the job goes to plan, $62.50 if it runs 50% long and loses $75.00 at double the time; time and materials at $135.00 an hour keeps earning as the clock runs but the customer bears the overrun. Neither is advice; it is arithmetic on the numbers you type.

vs-time-and-materials.html.text:
Plumber Flat-Rate Price Calculator · comparison

This calculator vs. time and materials

Short answer: time and materials bills the hours that happen; a flat rate bills the hours you promised. The calculator prices the flat rate from your true cost and shows the clock bill next to it, so you can see how far a job can run before the flat price stops paying.

Everything below is arithmetic on invented numbers and names no company or software product. Not business, tax, legal or licensing advice. No warranty.

What time and materials is

You bill an hourly rate for the time worked, usually with travel, plus parts at cost and a markup. The customer does not know the total until the work is done, and you are paid for a slow job and a fast one in proportion to the clock. It is the simplest thing to explain on a call and the hardest for a customer to compare with another quote.

What a flat rate is

A price agreed before the work, from a price book: the same job, the same number. It moves the risk of a long job from the customer to you, and the reward of a fast job from the customer to you. Customers can compare it; you must know your cost to set it.

The same job both ways

The default job is 2 hours on site, 0.75 hours of travel and $120.00 of parts, at a true cost of $100.00 an hour. The flat price is $595.00. On the clock at $135.00 an hour the bill is 2.75 x $135.00 + $198.00 of parts = $569.25. The two bills match at 2.94 hours.

Which to use

  • Flat rate suits repeatable jobs you have timed: toilets, faucets, water heater swaps, drain clears.
  • Time and materials suits discovery work where nobody knows what is behind the wall; many shops quote a diagnostic flat and the repair after.
  • Whichever you use, the clock rate should clear your true cost: at $90.00 an hour against a $100.00 cost every hour loses money, and the calculator says so.

Check your local licensing and written-estimate rules for how a price must be quoted.

Common questions

Is flat-rate pricing better than time and materials for a plumber?

Neither is better on its own; the difference is who carries the hours. On the default numbers the flat price is $595.00 and time and materials at $135.00 an hour bills $569.25 at the planned 2.75 hours, so the two bills match at 2.94 hours.

What does a flat-rate price cost me when a job runs long?

At 4.125 hours, 50 percent over plan, the flat price of $595.00 leaves $62.50 against $222.38 on the clock. At 5.5 hours it loses $75.00 while time and materials still earns $270.50.

When does flat rate pay better?

When you finish faster than the book time. At 60 percent of the planned hours the flat price leaves $310.00 against $135.75 on the clock, and the customer pays more than the clock would have charged.

Is this advice?

No. It is arithmetic on invented numbers; check every figure against your own records. Not business, tax, legal or licensing advice. No warranty.
